speaker: The Chairman
text: Head L, Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head L of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We have witnessed its far-reaching effects in many countries, from droughts and floods to bush fires.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We are fortunate that thus far, we have not had to grapple with direct effects of natural disasters caused by climate change.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, being a huge importer of food products, we are at the mercy of the global situation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hygiene and food safety are essential to sustainability of food sources.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In recent years, there have been several high-profile instances of food hygiene lapses.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How does SFA balance strengthening the food hygiene regime without causing an rise in business cost?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How does SFA ensure that the food industry continue to build a strong food safety culture even as globalisation and technological advancements transform the food landscape.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The battle to reduce plastic usage is essential for environmental sustainability.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is something new to everyone and, certainly, some companies will require more than a little guidance in the initial stages of implementation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Does the Ministry have plans to work with the industry to provide support for affected companies?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will the framework be tailored accordingly to different industries?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will it be applied to only local businesses, or also extended to imports, and how will that be implemented?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Packaging is often used for branding and marketing purposes.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some local businesses will likely proclaim the competition to be unfair if the imported goods may maintain their fancy and more aesthetically appealing packaging with little or no penalty.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I also note that with the COVID-19 outbreak, many sanitation products were frequently out of stock.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Were F&B businesses and places, where food is served or handled, affected by the shortages, and how did they cope with it?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How do we ensure enough supplies especially for hygiene in public toilets?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On the subject of food, food waste remains a significant problem.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are there measures in place to help the industry comply with the requirements?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Do hawker centres, coffeeshops, supermarkets fall under this regulation?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will this cause an increase in operation costs?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the last two years, many people were affected by food poisoning incidents as a result of improper hygiene and cleaning practices at places such as pre-schools and food establishments?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How do we foster greater responsibility by businesses and society to raise cleanliness and hygiene standards in Singapore?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Each and every Singaporean must regard environment conservation as our duty.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We may be a small dot on the globe, but we are heating up twice as fast as the rest of the world, as a result of the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As an island-city, it is inevitable for us to have many urban surfaces like buildings and roads.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Heat generated from our large, high-density population gives rise to UHI effect.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We need to reduce the rate at which we are heating up.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Government has been working very hard to increase the amount of greenery on our island, which has offered some relief from the heat.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am grateful to NParks for the intensified greening in Singapore in general and Yishun, in particular.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: With the increase in number of trees and bushes, the area has become a much cooler and more pleasant environment for the residents.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We are starting to see some new innovative green architecture around the island and I hope some of the existing buildings and infrastructure may soon get a makeover as well.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Doing so will stimulate even more innovation and creativity in the building industries.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I believe our implementation of photovoltaic (PV) systems could be more extensive.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I really like what Khoo Teck Puat Hospital has done with their roof tops, which is an energy-saving, green and sustainable combination of community gardens, farms and PV.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Moreover, PVs, with their large, flat surfaces, could be designed for multiple functions, such as providing shelters from the sun and rain aside from collecting energy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They could be designed to complement the aesthetics of the buildings they serve.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Climate change is a crisis but the Chinese term for crisis "危机" is also made up by two characters, which means danger and opportunity.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are plenty of opportunities if we set our minds to adopting bold changes and strategies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Climate change is now a major concern for many world leaders.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If we can set an example and come up with viable solutions to address climate challenges, Singapore would stand among the world leaders in addressing this major crisis, thus securing our relevance in the globe.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There is clearly a lot of local talent in our country.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can we pool their expertise together so there is a more coordinated approach and sharing of resources?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There is also plenty of talent and expertise.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Together, let us make this little red dot a shining example to the world.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And I am also very proud to be an engineer.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Dennis Tan, take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: According to NParks, this is due largely to land conversion from forests and other vegetated areas to settlements.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is particularly concerning, as over the past few years, we have seen the prioritisation of development projects over the benefits afforded by sensitive eco-systems due to such projects as the Cross Island Line, the Tengah HDB project and the Mandai project.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the Government be committed to securing the inviolability of our nature reserves and greater protection of the little that is left of our more natural green eco-systems in the future?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Apart from the forest significant heritage and ecological value, they provide Singapore with carbon sinks, important in our urban environment and helps mitigate the urban island heat effect.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also understand that Singapore uses satellite images covering all land use classes and the five carbon pools, as defined by the Inter-governmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) and have established permanent sampling plots across the nation for the tracking of carbon in relevant land use classes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the forest restoration action plan, as announced by NParks in January 2019, help in converting land in Singapore back to a net absorber of carbon?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Around three-quarters of these industry sectors emissions come from the oil refining and petrochemical sector.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Industrial energy efficiency, particularly for large emitters is currently being addressed by the Energy Conservation Act (ECA).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Large emitters are required under the ECA to submit annual energy efficiency improvement plans.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: From 2021, these emitters must also establish facility-wide energy management systems and conduct energy efficiency opportunities assessments which must be submitted to NEA.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the public have access to aggregated information on the improvements?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Minister Masago said in his Parliamentary Question reply to me last month that the Government works closely with the oil refining industry to ensure that they achieve high standards of energy efficiency and adopt sustainable practices; and that all three oil refineries in Singapore have set up co-generation plants, which can significantly improve the energy efficiency of the refineries.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Has the Government set any projection or targets for emissions reductions for our refining industry in the next five years?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And if not, will the Government consider doing so?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What we need now is the commitment by Government and businesses to actually reduce emissions and track it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Australia, carbon neutral certification under the Climate Active Carbon Neutral Standard is an example of how the government supports businesses as they account for and reduce carbon emissions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Energy Conservation Act currently requires large energy users in the industry and transport sectors to monitor and report energy usage and conduct energy efficiency assessments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A similar framework can be applied to carbon emissions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should, in the journey to halving greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, require all Government bodies and large companies to conduct annual carbon auditing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are a variety of carbon management services available in the market today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With carbon auditing, organisations can understand their greenhouse inventory, isolate each emission source, and hence, determine and model emission reduction strategies, their payback and viability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To help ease organisations into this, the Government could implement carbon auditing subsidies for the next 10 years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If companies successfully reduce their carbon emissions year on year, incremental subsidies can incentivise them to continue to do so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Other ways to encourage a greener report card could be doubling on handouts for low-carbon initiatives and progressive carbon tax relief.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More has to be done and decisively so, or the climate emergency will continue to worsen.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Louis Ng, you can take all your cuts together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These included incentivising solar energy, which is the most viable clean energy source in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should all move towards being fully solar powered.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will MEWR provide incentives to encourage solar deployment on rooftops and also provide consumers with rebates for electricity plans that use solar energy?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will MEWR also deploy more floating solar panels at our reservoirs?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad we have introduced the carbon tax to fight climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, the current $5 per tonne carbon tax rate is too low.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The timeline for reviewing the rate is also too long.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Young PAP and climate activists hope we bring forward the 2023 review and increase the rate to more than $15 per tonne.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, MEWR has said that it will not disclose the carbon tax contributions of companies because the tax was meant only as a price signal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Releasing emissions data by company and facility is not a new idea.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The EU publishes the emissions of 15,000 facilities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The UK requires its 2,000 listed companies to declare their emissions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What I am proposing is a carefully targeted measure.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We publish only the data of those that pay the tax.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means only the highest emitters will face pressure.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It also means they can stop being published by cutting their emissions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MEWR says the Carbon Pricing Act does not allow release of the data.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If that is true, we can amend the Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The fight against climate change should be built on transparency.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will MEWR study the idea of releasing emissions data on taxable facilities and companies?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, it is positive news that we have committed to having a fleet of local public buses that runs on cleaner energy by 2040.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is also good news that we intend to phase out internal combustion engines (ICE) and have vehicles run on cleaner energy by 2040.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But this will take time as we need to expand the charging infrastructure for electric vehicles.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the meantime, we can steer Singapore towards an environmentally-friendly car society by improving the Vehicular Emissions Scheme (VES).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, a hybrid car costs more – a lot more.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Ministry consider offering higher rebates under the current VES and increasing surcharges for vehicles with higher emissions?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that we are not in the business of making cars cheaper, but we are in the business of protecting our environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can do this by urging people and steering them towards purchasing hybrid cars in the next 10 years, again before the charging infrastructure for electric vehicles is ready.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is also good news that we will be extending the VES to light commercial vehicles.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), commonly used in refrigerators and air-conditioners, are greenhouse gases that contribute to global warming.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: NEA has put in place licensing controls for the import, export and manufacture of 18 types of HFCs which took effect from 1 January 2019.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, Singapore has not yet ratified the Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol which requires parties to phase-down the production and consumption of HFCs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Ministry share whether Singapore will ratify the Kigali Amendment and share its plans to further reduce the use and emission of HFCs in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Temasek has taken a strong lead in tackling climate change and is urging everyone to join them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Mdm Ho Ching said a few months ago, "Some businesses have already planned for 100% renewable energy before or by 2050.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Others are setting yearly goals to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For those of us who have not started, I propose that we take a simple step, to report our electricity and transport usage by next financial year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is very simple; whether you are big or small, it is a very simple step to take.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is a proxy for our indirect emissions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Once we track and measure, as all businesses know, we can start to scope our solutions to reduce emissions or reduce waste." Can the Ministry follow Temasek and take the very simple step of reporting its electricity, paper, travel and water usage?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Public Service also follow Temasek and pledge to go carbon-neutral by this year and, like Temasek, ensure that “Sustainability is not just one of our roles.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We no longer use disposables at Nee Soon East CC events.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This year, we will expand it to all our RC events.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, it is shocking to me that we have used so much in less than a year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If we can save so much in Nee Soon East, imagine how much we can save if more were to join us on this "Say Yes to Waste Less Journey".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know that MEWR is already doing this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the entire Public Service commit to end the use of all disposables at all Public Service events?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr Chairman, high usage of air-conditioning and refrigerators contributes to global warming, and none more so than in Singapore where we love our climate control and air-conditioning.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But as a responsible member of the global community, we should do our best to reduce our carbon footprint.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Ideally, our cooling appliances should be energy-efficient and operate using refrigerant gas with a lower global warming potential.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many refrigerants have a global warming potential that can be over 1,000 times as potent as carbon dioxide.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How will the Ministry help our consumers make more climate-friendly choices for their household appliances?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, I will be focusing on the two funds created in Budget 2020.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: My questions are related to these policies and I commend MEWR for taking this step to set up these two funds in its fight against climate change.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Will any funds be allocated towards understanding the pollutive effects of each industry and reducing the levels of pollution?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, are there any plans to incorporate sustainability as a factor in our Industry Transformation Roadmaps?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The next questions on the SG Eco-Fund flow from my concerns regarding the Coastal and Flood Protection Fund.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: What sort of projects does the Ministry expect to fund using this fund and how does this differ from the Coastal and Flood Protection Fund?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: What sort of measurable impact does the Ministry expect that this fund will have?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, what plans does the Ministry have to co-create sustainability with Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It is very important that we bring Singaporeans onboard this entire journey and process and allow us to help them co-create the future.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I wonder whether these funds or any funds are available to create "green" jobs and equip our fellow Singaporeans with the skills needed to support our paradigm shift in sustainability.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Specifically, how will the investments mentioned above support our economy?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: What steps is the Ministry taking to open up opportunities for industries and our workers in Singapore?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As an island state, sea level rise is an existential issue for Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can the Minister provide an update and details of the plans to build up our coastal defences?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: And as building coastal defence against sea levels would likely involve multiple agencies and stakeholders, can the Minister also provide details of the Government's strategy to coordinate our coastal protection efforts?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Since Singapore's Independence in 1965, we have faced two primary water management challenges – scarcity of fresh water and flood risk.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As a low-lying country, we faced the threat and damage of inland flooding.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At the same time, we need to manage our scarce water resources well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: History shows floods have had a long-running effect on Singapore – national records remind us of the extensive floods in Newton Circus in December 1969, Rochor Canal in November 1973 and Braddell Road in December 1978.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have certainly come a very long way.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: From 2013, there have been several flash floods with floodwaters up to half a metre deep.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With climate change picking up, Singapore will experience increasingly extreme and unpredictable weather, probably resulting in more frequent and intense storms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What are PUB's future plans to mitigate against inland floods in the face of this challenge?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Have these helped to prevent floods and strengthen Singapore’s flood resilience?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Are there any more of such major drainage projects that PUB plans to undertake?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In addition, how do we tackle flood risk and balance this against societal affordability?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could other cost-efficient options, including green infrastructure, green areas that retain rainwater and mangrove restoration, be further reviewed?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How is the Government also getting the commercial property developers to do their part for flood mitigation?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Also essential are monitoring and public communication systems that alert populations to flooded areas, such as the ones PUB has developed, to provide early warning of risky, flooded areas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The severity and enormity of the challenge requires us to plan way ahead but execute quickly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What is the progress of the Ministry’s efforts and what are the concrete measures that have already been embarked upon?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: When can the public expect to see the overall blueprint?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Coastal protection will require balancing of varying needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, protecting our coastlines with sea walls and polders might have permanent ecological impact.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It might have impact on shipping lanes, underwater cable infrastructure, maritime security and international relations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is extensive work that cuts across multiple agencies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would the Ministry consider setting up a one-stop agency to coordinate Coastal Protection work?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Coastal Protection and Flood Mitigation can also bring about significant economic opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While we learn extensively from the Dutch experts on, for example, polder work, how are we localising such knowledge?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Are we also building up a pipeline of local talent in such work so that it might result in another "Water Story" for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Because of the vast capital needs of such projects, local companies might not be able to participate in this important national project.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How is the Ministry ensuring that our local firms can participate and that there is sufficient technology transfer?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What principle would be used for financing such projects, noting the need to balance inter-generational needs?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Lastly, dengue has become a tropical disease that we have to live with.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Because of climate change, Singapore is experiencing warmer temperatures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How does this affect our longer term dengue management strategy?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While COVID-19 takes our immediate attention, dengue continues to be a persistent challenge that also deserves significant attention.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, dengue case numbers for the beginning of this year have spiked against the same period last year and there are several live clusters in certain estates in Aljunied GRC.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Residents remain concerned even as they appreciate the diligence of NEA teams in the area.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The warmer weather in the coming months could lead to an even higher mosquito population.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In terms of anti-dengue strategy, there was previous discussion about the prospects of a dengue vaccine.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, recent experience from other countries which have tried a vaccine has cast doubts about its efficacy and highlighted potential health risks.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Controlling the mosquito population may have better and more immediate prospects.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Project Wolbachia is a promising technology for vector control, where infected mosquitoes are deployed for sterile breeding.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The project has been expanded in Singapore but it is still under study and is not deployed in existing dengue clusters.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Long-term, with climate change and global warming, mosquitoes are poised to breed faster, and the virus replication may also be accelerated.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the light of these developments, has the Government adjusted its dengue containment strategies, both short-term and long-term?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Also, how has NEA coped with the manpower challenges of such outbreaks and leveraged technology to augment its manpower?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Health and Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Warmer temperatures can potentially lead to an increase in mosquito population and spread of vector-borne diseases, including dengue.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Health and Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: How will the impact of climate change affect dengue management?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Health and Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: This year, the number of dengue cases is concerning.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Health and Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: There is an increasing number of dengue cases of serotype 3.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Health and Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Singapore needs to be vigilant and be on the alert.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Health and Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Can the Ministry share any new plans for dengue management?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Health and Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: How does Project Wolbachia fit into these plans?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Chairman, even as we battle the COVID-19 outbreak, another health threat is already facing us and it has been facing us for a long while.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Since the beginning of the year, the number of dengue infections has been increasing.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Even as I speak, my constituency of Queenstown has three active dengue clusters and one could argue that the dengue problem could pose an even larger and more real threat to Queenstown and to the rest of Singapore than even COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Singapore has been seeing warmer temperatures in recent years as a consequence of global warming, punctuated by more frequent showers, which provide fertile grounds for mosquito breeding.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: How will the impact of climate change affect our dengue management strategies?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: What are the Ministry’s plans for dengue management in the future and how does Project Wolbachia fit into our national strategy to combat the dengue menace?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Will the Ministry please provide an update on the project to date and whether it would be expanded to other areas in Singapore?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: In addition, I would like to ask whether the Ministry is satisfied with the results of our public education and campaign to prevent mosquito breeding?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: And how have industries and households responded to enforcement measures?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Ng, take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It is good news, but many residents still have concerns about this project.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Many ask me why we are releasing mosquitoes that will bite them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I tell them we are only releasing male mosquitoes and "Males don’t bite".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The next concern is that they tell me the males will attract the females who will then bite them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I tell them do not worry, it is the males who look for the females.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can MEWR share how we will be increasing awareness about this Project and also whether there are further plans to expand this to other parts of Singapore so more people can benefit from it?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Food waste is a serious and growing problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: At the same time, some Singaporeans struggle to have three meals a day.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Both problems can be alleviated if we introduce a Good Samaritan Food Donation Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This piece of legislation would help encourage companies and organisations to donate healthy food that would otherwise go to waste.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It will help both the environment and our people.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Will MEWR support a Private Member's Bill for a Good Samaritan Food Donation Act?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, the COVID-19 crisis highlights the importance of having diverse sources of supply for all our imported goods.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore is particularly vulnerable since we are so reliant on imports.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is natural to want to order more from particular trading partners which are reliable and offer good value for money.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, this will consequently reduce the imports from other sources.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry provide an update on how it ensures a robust import strategy to prevent supply disruptions, price hikes and supply fluctuations?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, as we import most of our food, we are vulnerable to external shocks that affect food supplies at their sources.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry share an update on how we could achieve the 30-30 goal and what measures and incentives are available to encourage Singaporeans to seize the new opportunities in our food production sector?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As such, Singapore is especially vulnerable to disruptions in the global food supply chain and to price fluctuations.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Deputy Prime Minister shared in his Budget speech that our imported supplies could also come under strain from climate change or geopolitical tensions.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In land-scare Singapore, our approach to realising our "30 by 30" goal must be meticulously planned and carefully calibrated.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is, therefore, important that Singapore focus on R&D to harness technological advances to boost local food production.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on what are the challenges and opportunities for Singapore associated with our goal?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can the Minister also share the progress on our vertical farming and fish farming?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: How can we reach our 30-30 goal and help our local agri-food sector grow sustainably in the long run?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Today, Impossible burgers is well received in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I just heard that we are going to have Impossible gyoza for tea later.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As we gravitate toward plant-based foods, SFA has a responsibility to ensure that they are safe for consumption.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: A framework is being set up by SFA to look into the safety assessment criteria of novel food.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There will also be opportunities for our food industry to grow our presence in this area.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can the Minister share how is SFA facilitating the business opportunities in this area while ensuring food safety is protected?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, take your two cuts, please.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: It is an ambitious goal as we only produce less than 10% locally today.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: To overcome our land, water and human resource constraints, we need to adopt innovative solutions and tap on technology to optimise productivity.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We will continue to need a lot of support from R&D.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: As food supply reliability is a fundamental national security issue, we must strengthen our resolve to make the endeavor a success.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on what the Singapore Food Agency (SFA) is doing to support our local farmers to help them succeed in the face of stiff competition in a free and open market?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: The launch of a SG Eco Fund by the Ministry to support partnerships with the community and enterprises in our sustainability efforts is much welcomed.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Indeed, Singaporeans are becoming more aware of the importance of sustainability in every aspect of our lives.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: From renewable energy to reducing plastic and e-waste, conserving our precious water resource to making sustainable food choices, we all hope to contribute in our own ways in the attempt to become a low carbon, low emissions country; and we are all putting in more effort into supporting sustainability efforts.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Can the Ministry share more details about the projects which Singaporeans and companies can apply for under this new SG Eco Fund?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: All of us can take action to reduce, reuse, recycle and refuse waste.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Twenty-nineteen was designated by the Ministry as the Year towards zero waste to rally Singaporeans to care for our environment and treasure our resources.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, very often, the bins are full and residents end up leaving their items around the bins.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The reason these bins fill up so quickly is that many plastic bottles and tins can be quite bulky, such as bleach bottles and Milo tins.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Add piles of newspaper and cardboard packaging waste, and the contributed items accumulate very quickly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, I would like to request that we increase the size of the bins or allocate more bins to each HDB block.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that their designs can also be improved to make them more user-friendly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some big items simply do not fit into the bin slots.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: We have an attitude of convenience and we depend on the Government to do everything.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: There is a conspicuous blue bin with simplified images showing what should be recycled at every HDB block and specially marked recycling trucks picking up the recycled thrash regularly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I think it is time we change strategy to turn the National Recycling Programme into community-led recycling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Experience in Germany, South Korea and Taiwan, which have the highest rates of municipal recycling, show that when urban communities are mobilised to take ownership of recycling programmes, cultures and norms of recycling become entrenched.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: In Taiwan, waste collection is not an individual throwaway chore but a community ritual and recycling party where piped music from waste collection truck bring out local residents with bags of recyclables and mixed waste, and community volunteers help residents sort out the thrash properly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: In Singapore, we have an urban set-up conducive for community recycling efforts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: With blue bins located at each HDB block, local grassroots organisations can take ownership of the bins to monitor the recycling trend of each block, diagnose problems such as low rate of recycling or indiscriminate dumping of thrash, and organise targeted events or campaigns to educate the residents of the block.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Mr Chairman, despite the move towards a greener, zero-waste nation, suppliers of fresh fruits and vegetables, meats and eggs as well as hawkers and cooked food sellers continue to use lots of styrofoam and plastic packaging.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: In COS 2018, citing Taiwan’s ban in single use plastics including straws, cups and shopping bags by 2030, I had asked about the Ministry’s plans to reduce the use of plastic disposables in Singapore involving either the restriction or the banning of single use plastic carrier bags, straws and disposable cups, containers and utensils.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: In 2016, the Government also said that it will not ban styrofoam products for food crockery and packaging but will seek to discourage hawkers from using disposable ware.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: We still see much styrofoam food crockery and packaging being used at hawker centres, coffee shops and other food outlets.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Given their harmful effects on the environment, I would also like to ask whether the Government will conduct a review of the use of styrofoam products for food crockery and packaging use, and whether it will set any target to ban such products or if not, what measures it will take to either reduce or to disincentivise such uses in the next five years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I will also like to ask whether the Government will be looking into encouraging alternative single-use products usage, such as bamboo products.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Using fewer plastic bags alone will not solve climate change or save the earth, but every bit counts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: And making us conscious of our habits, and consider better alternatives, has value in itself."  I agree with Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I have been calling for a plastic bag charge since 2018.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This is for all single-use bags, not just plastic bags.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Chairman, all Members of this Chamber agreed that climate change is an existential threat to our nation.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: To tackle this, I am heartened that last year, 2019, it was designated as Singapore's "Zero Waste Year", and we passed the Resource Sustainability Act (RSA), designed to promote resource sustainability.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: My following set of questions relates to the reflection of these priorities in Budget 2020.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Can the Ministry share the progress on this front?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Namely:  One, how many operators have applied for a license thus far and how many have been licensed?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Two, do we have sufficient local recycling capabilities to treat the expected volume collected e-waste?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: What measures is the Ministry taking to ensure the proper treatment of all e-waste collected?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: And three, given our focus on transiting into a circular economy, are there any plans to expand our Producer Responsibility Schemes beyond just e-waste; and by 2025, perhaps, packaging waste?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Four, what sort of progress has been made on the EPR scheme for packaging waste.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: What sort of support for affected companies will the Ministry be providing to ensure accurate data?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Additionally, the framework merely requires reporting, even if they cross prescribed thresholds.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Are there any plans and funds for the Ministry to work with the producers to implement their 3R plans?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Can the Ministry share if the scope of affected premises and thresholds have been determined?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Are there measures in place to help the industry comply with the requirements?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu, please take all your three cuts together.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Mr Chairman, packaging forms a significant portion of the waste that is generated by domestic sources, which include households and trade premises, such as shophouses.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Statistics from NEA show that one-third of our waste is packaging waste and 55% of that packaging waste is plastic.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Considering that only 4% of our plastic waste is recycled, there is certainly potential to further reduce packaging and plastic waste.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The Ministry had earlier announced plans to put in place an Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) framework to deal with packaging waste, including plastics, no later than 2025 or, perhaps, even earlier.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Under the EPR approach, producers bear the responsibility for the collection and treatment of their products when they reach end-of-life.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Would the Ministry share more details about how NEA intends to implement and enforce these plans?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: I am very happy with the Resource Sustainability Act which was passed last year.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: It is, I feel, one of the most important pieces of legislation introduced to deal with the increasing amounts of e-waste, food waste and packaging waste, including plastics, due to their quantities and low recycling rates.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The Act will give effect to the EPR scheme for e-waste.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The Ministry announced that a Producer Responsibility Scheme (PRS) Operator will be announced to collect and ensure proper treatment of regulated electrical and electronic consumer products on behalf of the producers.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: For non-consumer products, producers will be required to provide free take-back of all end-of-life commercial, industrial and electrical equipment before consigning them to licensed waste collectors or e-waste recyclers.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Would the Ministry share the progress of the scheme's implementation for e-waste?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: With the introduction of the Resource Sustainability Act last year, the EPR scheme will commence and a PRS operator I alluded to earlier will be appointed to collect and ensure proper disposal of electrical and electronic consumer products.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: For non-consummable products, producers will have to take back and transfer the equipment to licensed waste collectors or e-waste recyclers.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: What measures will the Ministry implement to ensure the proper treatment and responsible disposal of all this e-waste that is collected?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Chairman, high-rise littering is a particularly dangerous offence which can cause serious injury or even result in death.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: I strongly urge the Ministry to utilise all available tools and technology at its disposal to prevent and deter this anti-social behavior.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Rigorous enforcement should be conducted and heavy penalties meted out to offenders.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: What has been done to curb high-rise littering and whether the Ministry will be deploying more advanced technology or investigative techniques, such as identification through DNA?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Could the Ministry also leverage more on the sense of shame, such as by increasing the visibility and duration of the Corrective Work Orders, to punish these high-rise litterbugs?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Chairman, amidst this COVID-19 outbreak, much has been said about social responsibility and public hygiene.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: From Town Councils to offices, disinfection and constant cleaning has become the norm.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This crisis affords us the opportunity to also reinforce the importance of social norms, such as in our hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For a number of years now, we have been promoting the concept of tray returns.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, we also see many previous innovations fall into disuse.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In many older hawker centres, you see automated tray-return belts that have been switched off; coin-return machines that do not work; tray-return stations becoming manual stacking stations for cleaners.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the same time, the role of the tray is also very much temporary.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many remove their trays out of habit and place dishes onto tables.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is also a socially irresponsible behavior, such as the spitting of food waste and bones onto table surfaces, not just during COVID-19, but on any other day.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Cleaners often do not have the adequate tools nor training to properly clean.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This reduces the workload of cleaners, promotes a clean hygienic eating environment and reduces the spread of diseases.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To further achieve this, the design of hawker centres will also have to adapt.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some older hawker centres still use round tables, which are not conducive for the use of trays unlike rectangular tables in newer centres.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Beyond COVID-19, I hope that this will promote better hygiene and social norms in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: In late 2018, the new management model of hawker centres came under public scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Key issues raised were high stall rentals and operating costs, including hidden costs, long working hours and harsh contractual obligations.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: MEWR previously announced a review of the SEHC model.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Can MEWR provide an update on the implementation of these improvements?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin
text: Will new hawker centres continue to come under the SEHC model?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Chairman, hawker centres are an important and integral part of Singapore life.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Not only do they provide affordable, accessible, hygienic and good quality food, they also serve as essential social spaces where Singaporeans and visitors can gather to enjoy a good meal.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Are we still on track to meet this target?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How is the Ministry ensuring that the hawker trade can be sustained and how can productivity in hawker centres be raised in the face of manpower constraints?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Would the Ministry also share an update on how well each of the new hawker centres are doing?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Does the Ministry have any plans to review and enhance the present schemes for this sector?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is supposed to be Socially-conscious Enterprise Hawker Centre (SEHC) instead of Social Enterprise Hawker Centre.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Among the feedback were, having to apply for leave in advance if they choose not to open their stalls; not having the freedom to adjust food prices; having to pay penalty fees for terminating their tenancy; and high rentals and auxiliary costs that the hawkers have to bear.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The matter was addressed at length in Parliament in November 2018 with the Ministry sharing details, measures and giving assurances to Members of this House that the Ministry will manage or resolve the matter.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It has been about a year and four months since then.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Hence, I would like to seek updates on the current situation of the SEHC scheme.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: If yes, what is the number of feedback received and what are among the most common ones.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Additionally, I would like to seek updates on the number of SEHC island-wide at the present moment.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I also would like to know whether the Ministry has conducted any recent survey or study in finding out the level of succession of stall owners operating under the scheme.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a new approach and, understandably, the model would require continual adjustments and evolve into a viable and sustainable model.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I must credit the Ministry and NEA for daring to try a new approach and taking the earlier criticisms of the model in stride, although not all are really fair criticisms.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: From my recent conversations with some of the stallholders at Bukit Panjang Hawker Centre and the residents there that patronised the hawker centre, most had given me positive reviews for the new food centre.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am sure we can continually improve and finesse the model so that it can better serve the stallholders and residents.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As NEA is now building a second hawker in Bukit Panjang town and within my constituency, I would like to seek an update whether there has been further review of the model and what are the further refinements that we can expect.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, MEWR has set up two hawker workgroups last year.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I would be interested to know what are their thoughts and recommendations so far.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I was one of those infected as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Dengue is endemic in Singapore because of the presence of Aedes mosquitoes, which are the vectors for dengue virus transmission.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, our strategy has very much been focused on vector control, in essence, to prevent Aedes mosquito from breeding as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a long-drawn battle and it requires constant vigilance on the part of everyone.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our environmental condition, especially our warm weather, also makes it conducive for such transmission.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Could the relatively warmer weather be the possible reasons for the surge in dengue cases in recent years?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And if that is the case, how will the impact of climate change affect our management of dengue prevention?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I commend the NEA for pushing the envelope and leveraging new technologies to tackle this serious threat to our public health.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having been a dengue patient myself last year, I know how it is like to live through the illness and, of course, the concern about fatality.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should spare no effort to minimise the cases of dengue in Singapore, not any less than how we manage COVID-19, and continue to seek new strategies to fight this virus.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will certainly help to alleviate the difficulties experienced by our hawkers due to the reduction in business from the COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of these hawkers are worried about the outbreak deepening and prolonging, especially with the news of the virus spread in other countries.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The spread will increase the risk of new imported cases from different sources.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry consider providing more reliefs, such as more rental rebates, in the event of the outbreak worsening?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: The efforts to tackle our environmental changes require significant investment and transformation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: We will probably lose some jobs but also create new ones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: We will clearly need new skills in diverse areas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Can the Ministry share what are these critical skills needed to support our journey towards a sustainable and climate resilient Singapore?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: While we have some expertise, such as environmental engineering in Singapore, this might not be sufficient to fulfil our ambitions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Many of these skills might not be supported by existing education pathways.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Furthermore, these are not traditional fields for Singaporean students.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: How does the Ministry plan to jumpstart and develop this field in our Institutes of Higher Learning?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: One way is perhaps to attract firms to set up their R&D facilities in Singapore to take advantage of our robust IP framework.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: As we move into more recycling, traditional waste management and recycling firms will need to transform.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Will the Ministry be able to share what are the new jobs that might be created?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: What new opportunities will be available to our firms?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: How would the Ministry support them in their transformation?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Second, the "30-30" food security target has excited many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Opportunities can include R&D, production, financing and entrepreneurship.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: What is the total economic value that we can generate if we reach our target local production?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: How many and what type of jobs can we expect to create in the Food Story space?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: How are we preparing our younger Singaporeans in their education towards working in these food-related industries as the target is only 10 years away?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: In our journey to be more sustainable, water and food secure, some workers in traditional industries will be adversely affected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: How is the Ministry supporting job re-design and helping these workers to find higher-value work in their current industries?

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Mr Chairman, firstly, let me wish Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and all the engineers in the House today, Happy Engineer's Day.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The United Nations (UN) has rightfully identified climate change as the defining issue of our time.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For Singapore, like many small nations, climate change is an existential challenge.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We feel its effects today, such as in rising temperatures and frequent extreme weather events.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Even the seasonality of Singapore's rainy and dry months is now difficult to predict.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Coupled with the frequent and heavy storms also brought about by climate change, low-lying areas of Singapore such as the East Coast may experience more flooding.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For all countries, climate change also threatens access to essential resources like water, food and energy.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These affect the security of our nation too.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: With this said, our history of overcoming challenges gives me the confidence that we need not despair when facing climate change.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will create innovative solutions for the hardest challenge, putting Singapore in the unique position we enjoy today.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Today, I will update on our plans in three key areas to address the challenges of climate change – first, mitigation strategies to reduce the emissions of greenhouse gases or GHGs; second, adaptation plans; and third, how we can work together, in our communities and as a nation, to collectively realise a more sustainable Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the Paris Agreement are pivotal multilateral agreements to address the global challenge of climate change.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It has spurred many countries, including those who are large emitters, to enact laws and transform their economies to meet their carbon commitments.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is therefore in the interest of small island states like Singapore, to support this multilateral framework of cooperation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For this framework to stand, every country, large or small, must do its share to reduce GHG emissions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Halving our emissions, even 30 years from now, is an ambitious target, because Singapore is naturally constrained in alternative energy.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is an attribute recognised even by the UNFCCC.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is a clear signal to the whole of industry that Singapore is moving towards a low-carbon economy, as we give no exemption.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Daniel Goh asked about the carbon tax and emissions reporting.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The carbon tax, as I mentioned in the past Parliamentary Question, is meant to provide an economy-wide price signal.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To achieve emissions reductions, rather than scrutinising individual companies, it would be more useful to know which sectors we should concentrate on.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The release of individual data could also be commercially sensitive.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: What are the major moves that my Ministry will introduce to further reduce our GHG emissions?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: First, we will implement a package of comprehensive measures to reduce the emission of hydrofluorocarbons, or HFCs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As Dr Chia Shi-Lu and Mr Louis Ng have pointed out, HFCs can be found as refrigerants in refrigeration and air-conditioning equipment, and could leak during installation, maintenance and disposal.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Some forms of HFCs trap a much larger amount of heat in the atmosphere than carbon dioxide.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: From next year, NEA will mandate the proper recovery, reclamation and destruction of spent refrigerants.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In addition, NEA will launch a new grant to support companies who want to make an early switch to more climate-friendly commercial water-cooled chillers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To Mr Louis Ng's question, MEWR will initiate a review on our ratification of the Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol later this year.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Besides HFCs, improving energy efficiency will have a major impact on emissions reduction.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have set an ambitious target to improve our industrial energy efficiency to 1% to 2% every year.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our industries are on track to meet this target, and we will continue to improve our energy efficiency rates.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Last year, NEA announced the Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards, or MEES, for industrial-chilled water cooling systems.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: From 2021, energy-intensive companies, including oil-refining companies, will be required to establish facility-wide energy management systems and conduct energy efficiency opportunities assessments.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In MEWR, we also live by our energy efficiency creed.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are on track to complete the development of Tuas Nexus by 2027.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Tuas Nexus carries out co-digestion of food waste and used water sludge to generate up to three times more biogas than conventional sludge treatment processes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This biogas will be used to generate electricity to power the plant and excess electricity will be exported back into the grid.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In addition, we will ramp up the generation of solar energy within MEWR.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if we can deploy more solar panels on reservoirs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This year, PUB will deploy two 1.5 mega-watt peak (MWp) floating solar systems at Bedok and Lower Seletar Reservoirs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The power generated from this system alone is sufficient to meet the energy of all our water treatment plants at local reservoirs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: With this, Singapore's waterworks will be one of the few in the world to be 100% green.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: PUB is also making strides towards improving the energy efficiency of NEWater and desalinated water production.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked if the Government can provide consumers with rebates for using solar energy.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Subsidies, such as rebates, distort the energy markets.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Pricing energy right will encourage the growth of renewable energy in a commercially viable manner and incentivise consumers to use electricity efficiently, avoiding wasteful consumption.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Instead of rebates, the Government has streamlined regulations and funded research to support higher deployment of solar.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: My Ministry also intends to be exemplary in optimising the water-energy-waste nexus.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will set out to generate sufficient energy from waste incineration and solar photovoltaic systems to power all of my Ministry's needs, especially in the production of water and the projected production of food.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In the long run, it is only with groundbreaking technology that we can make huge leaps in climate mitigation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In the horizon are carbon capture, utilisation and storage technologies, and the use of hydrogen as an alternative fuel.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Beyond the Ministry, the Public sector as a whole is doing more.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In 2017, we launched the Public Sector Sustainability Plan, which charted out our strategies to reduce electricity and water consumption, and achieve Green Mark standards for 100% of our buildings.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Ministries and agencies are working hard, and are on track to meet our 2020 targets.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For example, all air-conditioned Government premises should maintain indoor temperatures of 24 degrees centigrade or higher where feasible.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: All Ministries have also taken the climate action pledge and committed to reducing their plastic, water and electricity consumption.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are reviewing how to bring our plan to the next level.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Deputy Prime Minister also announced our vision for all vehicles to run on cleaner energy by 2040.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: MINDEF, for example, will replace 400 administrative vehicles with hybrids and later, with electric ones when charging infrastructure is ready in 2040.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Together, with net-zero buildings, food waste management, our Army is "green" in more than in their uniforms.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This are but a few examples of what I said earlier in my speech on how the UN Climate Change Framework is shaping climate-conscious behaviours and decisions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are also reviewing other measures such as the better management of carbon emissions and the use of disposables.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: More details will be announced later this year.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Chairman, public transport generates up to three times less carbon dioxide than private transport.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Hence, our approach is to encourage public transport and green public transport as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Land Transport Master Plan 2040 by the Ministry of Transport (MOT) supports this.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is how Singapore moves to cut GHG emissions – simply drive less.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: If driving less is, somehow, not an option, motorists can still practise sustainable consumption by choosing cleaner vehicles that emit less GHG and harmful pollutants.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the Vehicular Emissions Scheme (VES).

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The VES implemented in 2018 has seen positive results and we have since extended the VES until end 2020.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This will complement the enhanced incentives and infrastructure to promote the use of electric vehicles announced at the Budget.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We aim to refine VES further, taking into account its impact on motorists' purchasing decisions and advancements in technology.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The transport of goods and services is a major economic activity in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Commercial vehicles, especially Light Goods Vehicles or LGVs, are key emission sources and pollute our air due to their high mileage and reliance on diesel.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To support the shift to cleaner commercial vehicles, we will introduce a new Commercial Vehicle Emissions Scheme (CVES) for new LGVs, which form the largest proportion of commercial vehicles.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In terms of Total Cost of Ownership, fleet owners will enjoy overall savings when they purchase EVs as opposed to petrol vehicles and even greater savings as compared to diesel vehicles.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The existing ETS will be extended until 31 March 2021.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Climate change will bring about more frequent and intense storms, which may result in major flooding, especially in low-lying parts of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked about PUB's plans to mitigate inland floods.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Since 2011, PUB has spent almost $2 billion on drainage works, including major projects like the Bukit Timah Diversion Canal and Stamford Detention Tank.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will invest another $190 million, with six projects commencing this year, including the construction of a detention tank underneath Syed Alwi Road, which will enhance flood protection in the Little India area.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our investments will be complemented with developments in technology, such as short-range radars, to better predict and manage heavier rainfall.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These efforts, however, will not be sufficient with climate change.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: With climate change, sea levels will rise faster than its natural cycle and along with heavy rains, will overwhelm drainage systems.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: With this new responsibility, one agency, PUB, will study both coastal and inland flooding holistically and develop models to guide our flood protection response.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The fund will be used in a fiscally sustainable manner to support the substantial capital outlay.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Mohamed Irshad asked about the immediate investments that will be made.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our near-term efforts will focus on studying our coastal areas to ascertain the type, feasibility and extent of measures required.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will phase efforts and start with the City to East Coast stretch and Jurong Island.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The funds will also be used to expand and improve our drainage infrastructure to improve flood resilience.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As we embark on coastal protection, we will also identify new opportunities for urban development.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For instance, we could reclaim a series of islands offshore, and even connect these islands up by building barrages to create community spaces for Singaporeans and contribute to water resilience.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: PUB will partner various stakeholders to explore these possibilities.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Dennis Tan highlighted the importance of preserving and building our carbon sinks.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will preserve our green carbon sinks and identify nature-based solutions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For example, planting mangroves can both stabilise our coastline by preventing erosion, while preserving our green lungs and supporting biodiversity.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Minister Desmond Lee will elaborate in his speech on Singapore's greening efforts.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Adaptation efforts also involve securing our water supply.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Singapore has developed a robust and diversified supply of water, as a result of our early and consistent investments in water infrastructure and research.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Along with local catchment and imported water, we will continue to augment our water supply with weather-resilient sources, namely, NEWater and desalinated water.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: With the completion of Marina East and Jurong Island desalination plants this year, we will have five desalination plants.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our NEWater production capacity will also increase over the next five years, with the expansion of the Changi NEWater factory and development of Tuas Nexus.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Good water demand management is equally important in complementing efforts in water supply.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: PUB's water conservation efforts have shown encouraging results, with household water consumption decreasing to 141 litres from 148 litres per person per day in three years.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: PUB will begin the deployment of 300,000 smart meters next year, as part of efforts to reduce water consumption further to 130 litres per person per day by 2030.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To inspire Singaporeans to continue efforts in water conservation, I am happy to launch the 2020 water conservation campaign.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I cannot do it now like the usual way, because of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Today, PUB will kick off with a new video to remind Singaporeans of how far we have come in our water story.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I feel touched and proud of our water story when I previewed the video.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So will you, when you watch it tonight.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It will encourage us, all Singaporeans, not to take our clean drinking water for granted.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Besides rising sea levels and water resilience, Mr Amrin Amin, Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Dr Chia Shi-Lu and Mr Desmond Choo have rightfully pointed out that warmer temperatures caused by climate change can also affect the everyday lives of Singaporeans, because it leads to an increasing mosquito population.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In fact, warmer temperature is one of the factors that led to the surge in dengue cases last year.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Project Wolbachia is a tool which NEA is piloting to manage the mosquito population.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
